summary:
Alone in Mars (MarsWalk) is an interactive 3D Martian mission planner and first-person extravehicular activity (EVA) surface simulator built around Jezero Crater. It unites an orbital telemetry and GIS dashboard with full-scale surface exploration, vehicle driving, and an interactive rover companion.

The platform fuses five NASA and USGS data layers—CTX/HiRISE elevation, terrain slope, hazard index, CRISM mineralogy, and THEMIS thermal inertia—into 17 mathematical models (M1–M17). Three routing engines (Classic A* O2, Multi-Dimensional Health A*, and a QAOA-inspired layered corridor) adapt to xEMU suit limits and crew physiology to guide parachute landing, sample collection, and MEDA dust storm evacuation.

Because Earth–Mars signals take up to 22 minutes each way, future explorers need autonomous, physiologically grounded survival maps, while students and educators gain an accessible scientific window into Martian operations.
details:
Local event: Puebla, Mexico.
Demo: MarsWalker on GitHub Pages
Repository: Cabezones-de-la-NASA/MarsWalker

MarsWalker connects an orbital planning dashboard to a playable surface simulation. The dashboard offers a detailed HiRISE window, two CTX views at different resolutions and a synthetic test crater. It derives slope and risk from elevation and displays points of interest when the selected dataset includes them. The EVA planner compares oxygen-cost A*, a weighted health route and a classical corridor heuristic inspired by QAOA. Users can adjust planning priorities, inspect an elevation profile and export the result as JSON.

On the surface, the helmet display tracks modeled crew resources and vitals, including oxygen and hydration. Players can explore on foot, rehearse a parachute landing or, in free exploration, drive a 6×6 with a first-person interior. Realism mode keeps surface time at 1× and removes the companion and vehicle. A simulated dust front changes visibility and wind. These mechanics let users rehearse decisions about terrain, effort, supplies and the return to shelter.

The front end uses JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Three.js 0.187.0 and Vite 8.3.8, with IBM Plex fonts, WebGL 2 and Web Audio. Python 3 tools prepare and validate terrain data. The project uses ESLint and Node’s native test runner. It runs in a WebGL 2 browser with compatible graphics hardware. A keyboard and mouse are recommended, and voice input depends on browser support and microphone permission. Adjustable graphics profiles help accommodate different hardware. GitHub Pages serves the static app, and the optional rover backend runs separately on Vercel.
